summary: Berkshire Hathaway Inc.’s 2023 Form 10-K cover identifies the company, fiscal year, incorporation, headquarters, contact details, NYSE-listed common shares and senior notes, and regulatory filing statuses. It reports nonaffiliate voting-stock market value and outstanding share counts, and incorporates portions of its 2024 proxy statement. The contents list covers business, risks, cybersecurity, properties, legal and mine-safety matters; equity and market information, management discussion, market risk, financial statements and notes, accounting and controls disclosures; governance, compensation, ownership, related-party matters, auditor fees, exhibits, schedules, and signatures.

title: Part I

nodes.title: Item 1. Business Description
nodes.summary: Berkshire Hathaway is a Delaware holding company headquartered in Omaha, with major insurance, rail, utility and energy businesses plus diverse manufacturing, service, retail and other operations. Management is highly decentralized; senior leaders oversee capital allocation, investments and operating-company CEO selection, while monitoring governance. The board oversees CEO succession, and the Code of Business Conduct and Ethics sets legal and ethical standards. At year-end 2023, Berkshire employed about 396,500 people worldwide (80% in the U.S.; 20% union-represented). Subsidiaries set varied workforce policies covering safety, compensation and benefits, wellness, training, advancement, hiring, diversity and inclusion. U.S. workforce demographics are published on the company website.

nodes.title: Insurance and Reinsurance Businesses
Insurance and Reinsurance Businesses (intro)
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s global insurance and reinsurance businesses, workforce, risk types, competitive factors, and underwriting-profit approach are described. The text covers U.S. and international insurance regulation, admitted and non-admitted markets, NAIC and IAIS standards, group supervision and capital reporting, Berkshire’s financial strength and ratings, and TRIA terrorism coverage, eligibility, deductibles, reimbursement, exclusions, and limits. It outlines international operations and Brexit-related arrangements, the underwriting groups and Alleghany’s integration, and GEICO’s products, distribution, competitors, market share, and exposure to claims variability.

nodes.title: GEICO
nodes.summary: The text describes varied non-U.S. insurance regulation, including licensing, solvency, reporting, local capital, records, privacy and U.S. legal requirements, and Berkshire’s post-Brexit Irish entity and London presence. It outlines Berkshire’s underwriting groups, Alleghany’s acquisition and segment placement, and its expectation of long-term underwriting profits while rejecting underpriced risks. GEICO’s products, direct marketing, competitors, market share, claims, regulation and weather exposure are covered, followed by the diverse U.S. specialty, commercial and professional insurers in the Primary Group. Finally, it explains BHRG’s global operations, constituent groups, reinsurance contract types and structures, and dependence on pricing and market conditions.

nodes.title: Property/casualty
nodes.summary: NICO offers property/casualty reinsurance on excess-of-loss and quota-share bases, catastrophe and facultative cover, and excess-of-loss primary insurance for large or unusual risks; its business volume varies with pricing and large transactions. A 20% quota-share agreement with Australia’s IAG was extended through 2029. General Re writes global, multi-line treaty and facultative reinsurance on quota-share and excess bases. Its North American operations include direct reinsurance through GRC and specialty and surplus-lines insurers serving public, commercial, and captive clients through selected intermediaries. International business is written directly and through brokers; subsidiary Faraday manages Lloyd’s Syndicate 435 and participates in all its results. TransRe provides treaty and facultative pro-rata and excess-of-loss reinsurance across P&C lines in the U.S. and abroad, mainly through brokers.

nodes.title: Life/health
nodes.summary: The text describes General Re’s global life and health reinsurance, including its 2023 regional premium sources, covered risks, traditional life reinsurance, and runoff variable-annuity guarantees. It explains retroactive reinsurance’s coverage, long-tail claims, pricing, expected underwriting losses, and investment benefits; BHLN’s structured-settlement annuities and 2023 business curtailment; and Berkshire insurers’ investment strategy, assets, and float growth from $123 billion in 2018 to $169 billion in 2023. It also outlines BNSF’s operations, workforce, network, freight markets and pricing, economic influences, and 2023 revenue mix.

nodes.title: Insurance Reinsurance, Annuities, and Investments
nodes.summary: BHLN and affiliates reinsure traditional life risks and certain closed-block variable-annuity guarantees. Retroactive reinsurance covers prior-event claims, often long-tail and subject to large limits; time value affects pricing, expected underwriting losses, and investment-funded economic benefits. BHLN’s structured-settlement annuities exchange upfront premiums for decades of payments, with expected losses from liability accretion; it sharply curtailed this business in 2023. Berkshire’s insurance investments, managed centrally, include concentrated public equities, fixed maturities, and short-term assets, without target allocations or liability-duration matching. Assets are funded by capital and float, whose components and growth from about $123 billion (2018) to $169 billion (2023) are described; float cost is measured by pretax underwriting results relative to average float.

Describes Berkshire’s global insurance and reinsurance businesses, regulation, financial strength, terrorism coverage, underwriting strategy, groups and Alleghany integration. Covers GEICO’s products, distribution, competition, claims and exposures; specialty and commercial insurers; and BHRG’s global operations and reinsurance structures. Details property/casualty operations at NICO, General Re, Faraday and TransRe, and life/health reinsurance, retroactive coverage and structured-settlement annuities. Also covers insurance investments, float and its growth and cost, plus BNSF’s network, freight markets, economic drivers and revenue mix.

nodes.title: Railroad Business—Burlington Northern Santa Fe
nodes.summary: BNSF, based in Fort Worth, operates a major North American railroad with about 37,000 employees, serving U.S. regions, ports, and parts of Canada and Mexico through its routes, shortline partnerships, and carrier marketing agreements. Its freight spans consumer, industrial, agricultural, and coal products; revenue and performance depend on contracts, published rates, and economic conditions. Federal, state, and Canadian regulators oversee rates, routes, acquisitions, safety, health, and environmental matters. Environmental rules and contamination risks can create significant costs and liability; diesel produces most baseline emissions, and BNSF targets a 30% GHG reduction by 2030 while pursuing fuel-efficiency, renewable diesel, battery-electric, and hydrogen technologies. Competition from railroads, trucking, barges, ships, and pipelines pressures prices and service, prompting efficiency improvements; Union Pacific is its main Western competitor.

nodes.title: Utilities and Energy Businesses
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s energy businesses include a 92% stake in Des Moines-based Berkshire Hathaway Energy. Berkshire invested 38.6% in Knoxville-based Pilot Travel Centers (PTC) in 2017, accounted for under the equity method until January 31, 2023, when an additional 41.4% gave Berkshire control and PTC became a consolidated subsidiary effective February 1. On January 16, 2024, Berkshire acquired the remaining 20%, making PTC an indirect wholly owned subsidiary. PTC primarily operates in fuel distribution and energy products and services.

nodes.title: Berkshire Hathaway Energy
General Matters
nodes.summary: Berkshire Hathaway Energy (BHE) is a global energy company with about 24,000 employees, spanning regulated U.S. utilities and gas pipelines, British and Canadian electricity networks, renewable-focused independent power projects, LNG facilities, and U.S. residential real estate businesses. Its four U.S. utilities serve about 5.3 million customers across diverse regions, own roughly 30,100 MW of generation capacity, and experience seasonal demand and revenue patterns. Three interstate pipeline companies operate about 21,000 miles of pipelines, storage facilities, and LNG assets, serving broad markets with seasonal demand variation. Other operations include British distribution networks serving 4 million users, Alberta transmission serving 85% of its population, approximately 5,900 MW of contracted power projects across multiple regions and technologies, and $7.3 billion invested in third-party wind tax equity projects.

nodes.title: Regulatory Matters
nodes.summary: U.S. utilities face extensive federal, state and local oversight. FERC regulates wholesale electricity, transmission, reliability, utility holding companies, records, securities, hydroelectric facilities and related matters, and may impose penalties; MEC is also subject to NRC regulation for its Quad Cities nuclear ownership. Utilities generally have exclusive retail service territories and service obligations, while some customers may choose alternative suppliers or self-generate. State commissions typically set cost-of-service retail rates, including a reasonable investment return, with bundled and transmission- or distribution-only options. UK Northern Powergrid distribution fees are formula-controlled for 2023–2028. Alberta’s AUC regulates AltaLink’s tariffs, rates, construction, operations and financing; AESO operates and plans the provincial grid. FERC regulates named interstate gas pipelines’ rates, services, facilities and LNG operations, while federal pipeline safety rules govern facility design, construction, operation and maintenance.

nodes.title: Environmental Matters
nodes.summary: BHE’s operations face extensive environmental laws covering air, climate, emissions, water and coal ash, with ongoing compliance duties and penalties. The text reviews evolving clean-air and clean-energy requirements; the Paris Agreement, U.S. withdrawal and reentry, and emissions pledges; court and EPA actions on power-sector greenhouse-gas standards; and finalized methane rules for oil and gas sources. BHE’s emissions mainly come from coal- and gas-fired generation. It reports renewable and storage investment, coal-unit closures, emissions reductions achieved by 2023, and plans for further investment and closures toward a 50% reduction from 2005 emissions by 2030.

nodes.title: Non-Energy Businesses
nodes.summary: HomeServices of America is a U.S. residential real estate brokerage offering brokerage and related services, including mortgages, title and closing, insurance, warranties, relocation, and other home services. It operates about 900 offices across 34 states and Washington, D.C., with 41,000 agents under 50 brands. Its franchise network has around 300 franchisees, 1,500 offices, and 48,000 agents, mainly in the U.S., using two brands and receiving support services for fees. Revenue depends on housing transaction volumes, typically higher in the second and third quarters; the business faces intense competition and general real estate market conditions.

Covers BHE’s global energy businesses, workforce, customer base, assets, generation and seasonal demand, including U.S. utilities and pipelines, UK and Canadian networks, contracted power projects, LNG and wind tax-equity investments. Describes federal, state, UK and Alberta regulation of utilities, electricity and gas operations, rates, safety and service obligations. Reviews environmental compliance, climate and emissions policies, renewable and storage investments, coal closures and emissions-reduction goals. Also summarizes HomeServices of America’s brokerage, franchise and related home services, footprint, revenue seasonality and market competition.

nodes.title: Pilot Travel Centers (PTC)
nodes.summary: Pilot Travel Centers operates over 650 travel centers, about 75 fuel-only sites, and diesel sales at more than 140 third-party locations across the U.S. and Canada, alongside major wholesale and fuel-marketing businesses. In 2023 it sold over 16 billion gallons of fuel, including low-carbon fuels and diesel exhaust fluid, opened EV charging stations under a GM network agreement, and pursued a Volvo truck-charging network; it employed about 26,700 people. Its highway-oriented centers serve travelers and truckers with fuel, merchandise, food, and amenities. The concentrated industry also includes Love’s and TravelCenters of America and smaller independents. Customer and supplier concentration is limited; PTC also has an oil-field water-disposal business. Environmental laws govern pollution and hazardous-site remediation, with penalties for violations, and certain assets create retirement obligations.

nodes.title: Manufacturing Businesses
Manufacturing Businesses (intro)
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s diverse manufacturing subsidiaries are organized into industrial, building, and consumer products groups. They produce industrial components and specialty products; homes and a range of building materials and components; and recreational vehicles, batteries, apparel, footwear, and other goods. The businesses employed approximately 184,000 people at the end of 2023.

nodes.title: Industrial products
nodes.summary: Precision Castparts (PCC), based in Oregon, manufactures complex components, alloys, fasteners, aerostructures, composites, and related products and services for aerospace, power and energy, and numerous industrial markets. Its investment-casting and forging technologies serve applications ranging from aircraft engines and airframes to medical, defense, energy, and industrial uses. Major customers include Boeing, Airbus, GE, Rolls-Royce, and Pratt & Whitney; sales largely follow orders or schedules under long-term agreements, which customers may terminate subject to payment for work performed. COVID-19 caused severe aerospace demand reductions through 2021; recovery began in 2022, with domestic travel above and international travel near pre-pandemic levels, while long-term demand forecasts remain strong. PCC faces competition from alternative manufacturing methods but cites its expertise, facilities, workforce, quality, and customer relationships as advantages. Its supply and costs are also exposed to geopolitical, labor, cartel, and inflationary pressures affecting scarce alloy metals.

nodes.title: Precision Castparts
nodes.summary: The text profiles three industrial businesses. Precision Castparts manufactures aerospace, power-generation and industrial castings, forgings, alloys, fasteners, aerostructures, composites, equipment and services; describes its technologies, markets, major customers, order patterns, post-COVID aerospace recovery, competition, constrained metal supplies and environmental obligations. Lubrizol’s Additives and Advanced Materials segments serve transportation, industrial, consumer and life-sciences markets worldwide; the text covers products, competitors, innovation and patents, sourcing, global operations and customers, recent disruptions, safety, investment, and regulatory and environmental risks. IMC is a leading multinational maker of precision carbide cutting tools, with numerous brands and manufacturing sites across several countries.

nodes.title: Lubrizol
nodes.summary: PCC faces evolving environmental laws and may incur significant future compliance and capital costs, especially for air, water and climate-related requirements. Lubrizol is a global specialty chemicals company with Additives and Advanced Materials segments, broad product applications, strong technology and patent capabilities, varied competitors, petroleum-based inputs, global operations and diverse customers. Disruptions have affected supply and operations; it invests in safety, reliability, cybersecurity and environmental compliance, while facing inherent regulatory, environmental and operational risks and potential liabilities. IMC is a major multinational carbide cutting-tool manufacturer with numerous brands and production facilities across several countries.

nodes.title: IMC International Metalworking Companies
nodes.summary: The text covers PCC’s exposure to evolving environmental laws and potentially significant future spending; Lubrizol’s businesses, products, markets, technology and intellectual property, raw-material sourcing, global operations, customers, disruptions, safety and environmental investments, and regulatory risks; IMC’s brands, carbide cutting-tool products, manufacturing and distribution, customers, competitors, tungsten supply risks, and environmental commitments; and Marmon’s global structure and six described business groups—foodservice, water, transportation, retail, metal services, and electrical—along with their products, operations, and markets.

nodes.title: Marmon
nodes.summary: IMC makes six categories of metal-cutting tools, especially engineered, consumable tungsten-carbide inserts, supported by global technical sales, diverse industrial customers, regional warehouses and ongoing product development. It competes with global and specialized manufacturers, relies on tungsten powder whose supply disruptions could raise costs, and commits to environmental compliance. Marmon is a Chicago-based global organization with 11 business groups and 100-plus businesses operating at about 400 facilities in 17 countries. Its groups cover foodservice, water, transportation, retail, metals, electrical, plumbing and refrigeration, industrial products, rail and leasing, crane services, and medical devices; Scott Fetzer companies join in 2024. Rail includes UTLX’s tank-car fleet and services and EXSIF’s tank-container leasing (including its 2022 Russia exit); crane activity is seasonal. UTLX serves diverse industries through long-term leases and high fleet utilization. Certain Rail and Medical businesses face government oversight, and Marmon monitors and remediates environmental matters in compliance with applicable laws.

nodes.title: Other industrial products
nodes.summary: The industrial products group includes CTB, a global agricultural and food-processing systems maker competing on price, quality, design, reputation and service, with adequate material supplies; LSPI, a global pipeline drag-reduction technology and services provider subject to environmental regulation; and W&W|AFCO, a 19-plant North American structural-steel fabricator with a substantial multiyear project backlog, acquired in 2022. Building products include Clayton, which offers factory- and site-built homes, financing and services, with substantial deliveries, backlogs and homesite holdings; it has faced input and labor constraints and higher-rate demand pressures, and operates under environmental and financial regulation. Shaw manufactures and distributes diverse carpet and hard-surface flooring, with integrated production, international operations, and project-management and installation services.

nodes.title: Industrial and Building Products Businesses
nodes.summary: The page describes LSPI’s global pipeline drag-reduction products and services, environmental compliance, and W&W|AFCO’s steel fabrication operations, projects, backlog, and 2022 acquisition. It covers Clayton’s factory- and site-built homes, sales and financing, production and backlogs, acquisitions, supply-chain conditions, housing demand, environmental compliance, and financial regulation. It also outlines Shaw’s flooring products, integrated carpet manufacturing, international operations, and project management and installation services.

nodes.title: Shaw
nodes.summary: The text profiles LSPI’s global pipeline drag-reduction technology and services, and W&W|AFCO’s 19-plant North American structural-steel business, projects, backlog, and 2022 acquisition. It describes Clayton’s factory- and site-built housing, sales, financing, backlog, expansion, input and labor challenges, market conditions, and regulatory obligations; Shaw’s flooring, turf, geosynthetics and solar products, manufacturing, distribution, raw materials, and competition; and Johns Manville’s insulation, roofing, fiberglass and nonwoven products, facilities, materials, research, and environmental regulation and compliance.

nodes.title: Johns Manville
nodes.summary: Shaw’s businesses include synthetic turf and patented environmental and solar solutions; its global wholesale sales, distribution network, carpet production, recycled inputs, raw-material costs, and flooring competition are described. Johns Manville’s products, markets, facilities, R&D, materials, environmental regulation, sales channels, competition, and seasonality are covered. MiTek’s global residential and commercial building operations, products, customers, and steel supply risks are outlined. Benjamin Moore’s coatings and brands, retail and Ace relationships, online sales, competition, raw materials, restored production, and environmental and worker-safety compliance are also discussed.

nodes.title: MiTek
nodes.summary: JM sells through contractors, distributors, retailers, manufacturers and fabricators; it leads key markets but faces large global, national and regional competitors, competing on value, differentiation, customization, product breadth, quality and service. Sales are moderately seasonal, peaking with construction activity in the second and third quarters. MiTek operates residential and commercial building businesses worldwide, with operations across 20 countries and sales in over 60. It leads in residential truss-market connectors, hardware, software, services and machinery, serving component makers and also commercial distributors and DIY retailers; hot-dipped galvanized steel supply and costs have historically fluctuated. Benjamin Moore makes premium coatings, emphasizes innovation and sustainable manufacturing, and sells varied premium and specialty brands through independent retailers, Ace stores, 72 countries, and online and account-order channels. Its Ace relationship, including private-label manufacturing, has expanded since 2019. Competition centers on quality, innovation, breadth, expertise, service and price, against paint retailers, manufacturers and major chains. Key raw materials have fluctuating availability and prices; pandemic-related constraints eased in late 2022 and were alleviated in 2023, restoring normal demand-aligned production. The company complies with environmental and worker-safety requirements and monitors or remediates known legacy environmental matters.

nodes.title: Benjamin Moore
nodes.summary: The text outlines JM’s sales channels, competition, product differentiators and seasonal demand; MiTek’s global residential and commercial building markets, offerings, customers and galvanized-steel supply variability; Benjamin Moore’s products, retail and online distribution, Ace relationship, competition, raw materials, recovered production, and environmental compliance and remediation; Acme Brick’s products, markets, facilities, seasonal and cyclical demand, raw-material resources, and compliance with air-emission standards; Forest River’s vehicle and boat products, dealer distribution, market concentration, share and safety regulation; and Fruit of the Loom’s apparel and sporting-goods brands, markets, manufacturing locations, raw materials, supplier changes, and competition.

nodes.title: Acme Building Products and Forest River
nodes.summary: Acme, based in Fort Worth, manufactures clay brick and concrete block and distributes other building products mainly to homebuilders and contractors across the South Central and Southeastern U.S. Its 12 brick plants and three Texas block facilities face seasonal, construction-cycle-driven demand; raw material supplies are considered adequate, and plants comply with current EPA MACT standards. Forest River, based in Elkhart, makes RVs, cargo trailers, buses and pontoon boats at facilities in six states, selling in the U.S. and Canada through independent dealers under multiple brands. The RV industry is competitive and consolidated; Forest River held about 33% market share in September 2023. It is subject to U.S. and Canadian safety rules, participates in a voluntary RV safety association, and believes its products materially comply.

nodes.title: Apparel and footwear
nodes.summary: The text describes Berkshire’s apparel and footwear businesses. Fruit of the Loom makes and distributes basic, casual and athletic apparel and sports equipment under several brands through mass-market, wholesale, department-store and sporting-goods channels. It performs much apparel production itself, with manufacturing and labor-intensive operations spread across the Americas, Asia, Morocco and Europe; some products are contractor-sourced. Its main inputs are U.S. cotton and polyester, and after 2021–22 supply disruptions it diversified suppliers, including for yarn services. Competition centers on features, quality, service and price. Garan designs and sells children’s apparel under owned and private-label brands, using subsidiaries in the U.S., Central America and Asia and U.S. distribution centers. Fechheimer makes uniforms for public-service and safety markets. BH Shoe Holdings makes work, outdoor, casual and western footwear across multiple brands; Brooks sells performance running footwear and apparel. Berkshire shoe businesses source significant volumes abroad and sell worldwide through retail, online, catalog and company-owned channels.

nodes.title: Other consumer products
nodes.summary: The consumer products group includes Duracell, a global battery manufacturer with production in the U.S., Europe and China, 31% of the alkaline battery market, broad retail distribution, and sufficient key raw materials; Jazwares, acquired in 2022, a toy and consumer-products company selling owned and licensed brands, virtual games, costumes and pet products in over 100 countries; Richline Group, whose five units make or distribute jewelry and other metal, gem and precious-metal products to retail, artisan and industrial markets; and Albecca, which operates in 13 countries, selling branded custom-framing materials and providing art printing and fulfillment services.

Berkshire’s manufacturing businesses span industrial, building and consumer products and employ about 184,000 people. Industrial operations include aerospace and specialty components, chemicals, carbide tools, Marmon’s diverse global businesses, agricultural and food-processing systems, pipeline technology and structural steel. Building businesses make homes, flooring, insulation, building components, coatings and bricks, with discussion of markets, operations, competition, supply chains, backlogs, seasonality and environmental and financial regulation. Consumer businesses include recreational vehicles, apparel, footwear and sporting goods, batteries, toys, jewelry and custom framing. The section also covers customer and distribution channels, market positions, labor and material risks, safety requirements, environmental obligations, and pandemic-era disruptions and recovery.

nodes.title: Service and Retailing Businesses
Service and Retailing Businesses (intro)
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s service and retail businesses employ about 55,000 people and span distribution, aviation, electronics, franchising, media, rentals and logistics. McLane distributes groceries, foodservice and beverages nationwide through three units, serving major retailers and restaurants. FlightSafety provides regulated pilot and aviation-professional training and manufactures simulators and training equipment. NetJets offers shared aircraft ownership, leases, prepaid cards and management services under aviation regulations. TTI distributes electronic components globally to diverse industries. Other businesses include XTRA trailer leasing; Dairy Queen restaurant franchising; Business Wire news distribution; CORT furniture rental and sales; WPLG television and digital media; Charter Brokerage logistics for petroleum and chemicals; and IPS global engineering, design and project services for regulated facilities.

nodes.title: Retailing Businesses
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s retail businesses employed about 26,000 people in 2023 and span automotive, home furnishings, jewelry, candy, kitchenware, party and educational products, and motorcycle apparel and equipment. Berkshire Hathaway Automotive operates 108 franchises at 83 dealerships, mainly in Arizona and Texas, plus collision centers, auctions, distribution, customer financing, and vehicle and insurance protection plans. The text describes its brands, competition, manufacturer and franchise agreements, and state protections. Home furnishings businesses NFM, R.C. Willey, Jordan’s, and Star offer furniture and related products across multiple U.S. markets, with their store, facility, and market footprints. Other retailers include Borsheims, Helzberg, and Ben Bridge jewelers; See’s seasonal confectionery business; Pampered Chef’s consultant and online kitchenware sales; OTC’s multichannel product brands and customers; and European motorcycle retailer Louis, with its product range, stores, and online sales.

Berkshire’s service, distribution, aviation, media, rental, logistics and retail businesses employ about 55,000 people, including 26,000 in retail in 2023. The section surveys McLane’s food distribution; FlightSafety and NetJets aviation services; TTI electronics distribution; and businesses in trailer leasing, restaurant franchising, news, furniture rental, television, logistics and engineering. Retailing covers automotive dealerships and related services, home-furnishings chains, jewelers, See’s candy, Pampered Chef kitchenware, OTC consumer products and European motorcycle retail, including their operations, markets, products and competitive or regulatory context.

nodes.title: Additional information with respect to Berkshire’s businesses
nodes.summary: The text directs readers to financial statement notes for segment revenue, pretax earnings, assets, securities, and investments. It reports Berkshire’s year-end 2023 ownership stakes in Kraft Heinz and Occidental, describes their businesses, and notes a 50% interest in Berkadia Commercial Mortgage LLC. It also explains that Berkshire’s reports and corporate materials are available online or free by written request.

nodes.title: Business Risks and Leadership Dependence
key_items: General Business Risks Terrorist acts could hurt our operating businesses.
Geopolitical events could cause losses to our business and losses in the values of securities we own.
We are dependent on a few key people for our major investment and capital allocation decisions.
nodes.summary: Berkshire and its subsidiaries face known and potential unknown business risks. Terrorism could cause casualties, property damage and operational losses. Cyberattacks may disrupt systems, compromise information, raise costs, impair operations or financing, and hinder competitiveness despite mitigation planning. Geopolitical conflicts and government responses could reduce sales, increase costs, disrupt supply chains, damage property or endanger employees. Major investment and capital allocation decisions depend heavily on Warren Buffett; Gregory Abel is the designated potential successor, and board oversight and experienced operating managers help mitigate succession risk.

nodes.title: Key Business and Financial Risks
key_items: We need qualified personnel to manage and operate our various businesses.
Investments are unusually concentrated in equity securities and fair values are subject to loss in value.
Competition and technology may erode our business franchises and result in lower earnings.
Unfavorable general economic conditions may significantly reduce our operating earnings and impair our ability to access capital markets at a reasonable cost.
Epidemics, pandemics or other similar outbreaks could hurt our operating businesses.
Regulatory changes may adversely impact our future operating results.
nodes.summary: The page outlines risks from difficulty recruiting and retaining qualified personnel; concentrated equity investments losing value and weakening shareholders’ equity, insurance surplus, ratings, and business capacity; competition and technological change eroding franchises; economic downturns, inflation, and constrained or costly capital-market access reducing earnings; epidemics and pandemics disrupting operations, demand, supply chains, counterparties, and markets; and regulatory changes increasing compliance costs or causing financial and reputational harm, including penalties for data-privacy violations.

nodes.title: Climate and Insurance Underwriting Risks
key_items: Climate change and the regulation of greenhouse gas (“GHG”) emissions may impact our businesses.
Risks unique to our regulated businesses Our tolerance for underwriting risk in our various insurance businesses may result in significant underwriting losses.
nodes.summary: Climate change and extreme weather may damage operations and increase insured losses, while new or stricter GHG rules could raise compliance costs—especially for BNSF and BHE—and regulatory noncompliance could harm results. The insurer’s willingness to assume substantial catastrophe risk can produce large losses despite underwriting controls; coverage exclusions may be unenforceable, reducing earnings. Long-tail claims, imprecise reserves, and changing legal or social conditions may expand liabilities beyond underwriting intent. Unpaid property and casualty losses totaled $146 billion at year-end 2023, and even a small reserve increase could materially lower earnings.

nodes.title: Changes in regulations and regulatory actions can adversely affect our operating results and our ability to allocate capital.
nodes.summary: Regulatory changes and enforcement may restrict Berkshire’s insurance businesses—including permitted coverage, pricing, capital, investments and dividends—and impair results or capital allocation. BNSF faces extensive rail regulation and compliance risks, potential costly changes, coal-policy exposure, hazardous-material liability, and limits on pricing or network investment. BHE’s heavily regulated utilities and energy operations face evolving rules affecting assets, operations, rates, financing and dividends; noncompliance or regulatory changes may materially harm results. BNSF and BHE require major long-term capital investment, whose costs may not be recoverable through rates; project failures and disrupted debt-market access could weaken earnings, liquidity and capital resources.

nodes.title: Item 1C. Cybersecurity
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s cybersecurity framework lets business groups tailor risk management while supporting consistent material-event reporting. CISOs report annually to group management and internal audit; groups report significant incidents and monitor third-party risks, which can cause financial, operational, or reputational harm. The Audit Committee oversees the program, incident trends, and IT/cyber audits; senior managers handle daily protection and assess SEC reporting. The properties section describes BNSF’s rail network across 28 U.S. states and three Canadian provinces, its tracks, facilities, equipment, and 2023 repair and maintenance expense of about $2.5 billion.

nodes.title: Cybersecurity Oversight and BNSF Properties
nodes.summary: Berkshire relies on third-party providers for information systems and monitors related cyber risks. The Audit Committee oversees cybersecurity through incident and trend reports and internal audit work; business-group management handles daily protection, reports significant events, and senior management considers SEC disclosures. The page describes BNSF’s rail network across the U.S. and Canada, including owned track and trackage rights, operating facilities and equipment, about 7,500 locomotives and 72,800 freight cars, and $2.5 billion in 2023 repairs and maintenance.

nodes.title: Utilities and Energy Businesses
nodes.summary: Berkshire Hathaway Energy’s assets support electricity and natural gas operations, including generation, mines, grids, pipelines, storage, LNG facilities, and related rights; most are pledged for subsidiary debt. The text lists generating entities and locations by energy source, capacity definitions and totals, projects under construction, and operating and planned battery storage. It describes the scale and locations of BHE subsidiaries’ electricity networks, gas distribution systems, pipelines, storage fields, and LNG facilities. Pilot Travel Centers operates about 600 travel centers and other fuel, ethanol, and oil-field businesses.

nodes.title: Other Segments
nodes.summary: The text summarizes physical properties across Berkshire’s business segments—insurance (GEICO and BHRG), manufacturing, services, McLane, and retailing—by country and U.S./non-U.S. locations. It lists property and facility types, including offices, claims and training centers, manufacturing and production facilities, warehouses, distribution centers, retail/showrooms, housing subdivisions, hangars, and leasing facilities, alongside counts of owned and leased properties.

nodes.title: Legal Matters, Mine Safety and Executive Officers
nodes.summary: Berkshire describes routine and other pending legal actions, including insurance-related claims and possible punitive damages, and says they are not expected to materially affect its financial condition or results; certain subsidiary litigation is discussed in Note 27. Mine safety disclosures appear in Exhibit 95. The page lists four executive officers—their ages, roles, and service start dates—and states their terms continue until a successor is qualified or they otherwise leave office.

summary: Part I describes Berkshire Hathaway’s organization, governance, workforce, decentralized management and succession, and its insurance and reinsurance, railroad, utilities and energy, manufacturing, service, distribution and retail businesses, including operations, markets, properties, regulation and environmental matters. It covers major investments and segment information; terrorism, cyber, geopolitical, personnel, investment, economic, pandemic, competition, climate, underwriting, regulatory and capital risks; cybersecurity oversight; unresolved staff comments (none); legal matters, mine-safety disclosures and executive officers.

title: FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS

nodes.title: Market Information
nodes.summary: The document explains that Berkshire forward-looking statements include predictive, future-oriented, and performance or strategy statements; they reflect current expectations, are subject to risks and uncertainties, do not guarantee results, and are not specifically intended to be updated. Actual outcomes may differ due to investment-price changes, derivative losses, catastrophes, epidemics or pandemics, legal or tax changes, and broader economic or market factors. It also states that Berkshire Class A and Class B shares trade on the NYSE as BRK.A and BRK.B.

nodes.title: Shareholders, Dividends, and Stock Repurchases
nodes.summary: As of February 12, 2024, Berkshire had about 1,200 Class A and 18,000 Class B record holders; nominees held substantial shares for beneficial owners. Berkshire has paid no cash dividend since 1967. Its repurchase program allows Class A and B buybacks below conservatively estimated intrinsic value, in market or private transactions, subject to a $30 billion minimum for cash, equivalents, and U.S. Treasury Bills. Fourth-quarter 2023 data lists monthly shares repurchased and average prices. The program has no share or dollar limit, obligation to repurchase, or expiration date.

nodes.title: Stock Performance Comparison and Reserved Item
nodes.summary: The stock performance graph compares the subsequent value of $100 invested in Berkshire common stock on December 31, 2018, with investments in the S&P 500 and S&P Property & Casualty Insurance indices. Index returns include reinvested dividends. Berkshire notes that its diverse businesses make a comparable peer group difficult to develop, so it uses the property and casualty insurance index for comparison. Item 6 is reserved.

nodes.title: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations Results of Operations
nodes.summary: The passage presents Berkshire Hathaway’s after-tax earnings by business for 2021–2023, noting noncontrolling interests are excluded and that non-controlled businesses include certain 20%–50%-owned entities. It describes the company’s decentralized management, senior leadership’s capital-allocation and CEO-selection roles, and uncertainty from COVID-19, geopolitical conflict, supply disruptions, and anti-inflation measures. It explains changes in insurance underwriting and investment income, BNSF, utilities and energy, and PTC earnings, including key causes and PTC’s transition from equity-method accounting to consolidation in February 2023.

nodes.title: Results of Operations
nodes.summary: Manufacturing, service and retail earnings rose 2.0% in 2023 after 12.5% growth in 2022, amid uneven results and weakening demand at some businesses; investment gains were volatile and included a $2.4 billion PTC remeasurement gain, while foreign-exchange gains also affected earnings. The discussion explains Berkshire’s separation of insurance underwriting and investing, catastrophe and reserve-estimate volatility, insurance operations and acquired Alleghany businesses, and expected losses on certain long-tail contracts. It reports underwriting results for GEICO, BH Primary and BHRG. GEICO’s 2023 earnings recovered as premiums rose and claims frequencies and prior-year estimates improved, despite higher severity; 2022 losses reflected inflation and higher claims. Rate increases and advertising cuts contributed to higher premiums per policy but fewer policies in force.

nodes.title: GEICO
GEICO (intro)
nodes.summary: The passage reports 2021–2023 insurance underwriting results, noting retrospective revisions to Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group figures. It details GEICO’s business model and results: 2023 underwriting recovery from higher rates, lower claim frequency, favorable prior-year estimates and reduced advertising, despite rising claim severity; 2022 losses from inflation and more frequent/severe claims; premium, loss, expense, ratio, policy-count, coverage-frequency/severity, catastrophe-loss and prior-year-development comparisons for 2023 versus 2022 and 2022 versus 2021. It also describes Berkshire Hathaway Primary Group’s commercial insurers and coverages, its expansion to include RSUI and CapSpecialty in October 2022, and its 2021–2023 premiums, losses, expenses and underwriting earnings.

nodes.title: GEICO Underwriting and Berkshire Primary Group
nodes.summary: Reviews GEICO’s 2023 claims trends, prior-year loss estimate reductions, lower underwriting expenses, and improved expense ratio. Compares 2022 with 2021, covering premium growth, policy declines, increased claims frequency and severity, catastrophe losses, prior-year estimates, and lower expenses. Describes Berkshire Hathaway Primary Group’s commercial insurance businesses and lists 2023, 2022, and 2021 premiums, losses, expenses, and underwriting earnings.

nodes.title: Berkshire Hathaway Primary Group (Continued)
nodes.summary: Berkshire Hathaway Primary Group premiums written rose 24.1% in 2023, mainly from RSUI and CapSpecialty, and 16.1% in 2022, reflecting growth across several insurers and acquisitions. Loss and adjustment expenses increased in both years, but the 2023 loss ratio fell 6.4 points as catastrophe losses declined and business mix changed. Prior-year liability estimates were reduced in 2023 and 2022, chiefly for medical professional liability and property; 2021 also had catastrophe losses and prior-year reductions. Workers’ compensation and liability claims carry severity, long-tail, and adverse-judgment risks. Underwriting expenses rose in both years, primarily with earned premiums and business mix, including the acquisitions.

nodes.title: Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group
nodes.summary: BHRG provides global property/casualty, life/health and retroactive reinsurance, plus periodic-payment annuities, through its subsidiaries; TransRe joined in October 2022. The text reports premiums and underwriting results for 2021–2023 and notes retrospective accounting adoption effects. Property/casualty premiums written rose 31.8% in 2023, including TransRe, reflecting new business and higher rates; catastrophe exposure makes results volatile. Losses rose overall, though the loss ratio improved, with catastrophe losses and favorable prior-year reserve development reported. Expenses increased, and expense-ratio changes reflected currency movements, business mix and TransRe; foreign-exchange gains or losses are detailed.

nodes.title: Life/health
nodes.summary: The life/health reinsurance results report premiums, benefits, expenses, and pre-tax underwriting earnings for 2021–2023. Earnings were $354 million in 2021, $109 million in 2022, and a $237 million loss in 2023. The 2023 results included a $134 million gain from commutations of U.S. life contracts, which reduced earned premiums by $164 million and benefits and expenses by $298 million. Excluding this effect, earned premiums were largely unchanged and life benefits fell 5.3% versus 2022; the underwriting expense ratio rose 3.0 percentage points, mainly due to commutations and higher expenses.

nodes.title: Reinsurance and Periodic Payment Annuities
nodes.summary: Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group premiums and life and health benefits declined in 2022, mainly due to currency effects, lower Asia-Pacific volume, and elevated 2021 pandemic claims. Retroactive reinsurance results reflect deferred-charge amortization, changing claim estimates, and currency movements; 2023 losses rose with higher asbestos, environmental, and casualty estimates. Unpaid losses and deferred charges declined, with amortization recognized over settlement periods. Periodic payment annuity volumes are price-sensitive; new business stopped after prices fell in late 2022. Results reflect liability accretion, currency effects, and a 2022 contract termination; year-end liabilities are reported, and a 2023 accounting standard requires quarterly discount-rate updates for life-contingent contracts, recorded in other comprehensive income.

nodes.title: Variable annuity
nodes.summary: Variable annuity guarantee reinsurance contracts, which have been in run-off for many years, generated pre-tax earnings of $233 million in 2023, $467 million in 2022, and $169 million in 2021; results are affected by volatile securities markets, interest rates, and foreign exchange rates. The text also introduces a summary of insurance-operation net investment income, including dividends, interest and other investment income, pre-tax income, taxes and noncontrolling interests, net investment income, and the effective tax rate.

nodes.title: * Not meaningful.
nodes.summary: The text reports investment income trends: dividend income fell in 2023 after rising in 2022, with changes driven by investment dispositions, dividend rates, and equity holdings; interest income increased in both years due to higher rates and Alleghany income. It describes insurance float, underwriting results, cash and investment balances, and fixed-maturity holdings and credit ratings. It also presents BNSF’s network, earnings, freight volumes, and 2023 results, including lower revenue and pretax earnings due to reduced volumes, fuel surcharges, and higher non-fuel costs.

nodes.title: Railroad
nodes.summary: Reports 2023 fixed-maturity investment holdings by category, amortized cost, unrealized gains or losses, and carrying value, noting strong ratings for U.S. and most foreign government obligations. Describes BNSF’s North American rail network and product groups, then presents 2021–2023 railroad revenues, operating expenses, earnings, taxes, and freight volumes by group with year-over-year changes. Explains that 2023 revenue and pre-tax earnings fell, chiefly due to lower volumes and higher non-fuel costs, partly offset by lower fuel costs and favorable price and mix.

nodes.title: Railroad
nodes.summary: The discussion reviews railroad results for 2023 versus 2022 and 2022 versus 2021, detailing revenue, volumes, pricing and causes across consumer, industrial, agricultural and coal products, plus operating expenses, expense ratios, fuel, compensation and other costs, and interest income. It describes Berkshire Hathaway Energy’s ownership, businesses and regulated-rate framework, presents consolidated earnings and segment results, and explains 2023 and 2022 performance for U.S. utilities, gas pipelines, other energy businesses, real estate brokerage, and corporate interest and other, including wildfire accruals, energy margins, tax credits, rate and volume effects, acquisitions, market conditions and expenses.

nodes.title: Pilot Travel Centers, LLC (“PTC”)
nodes.summary: Pilot Travel Centers, LLC (PTC) operates Pilot and Flying J travel centers, fuel-only retail locations, and major U.S. wholesale fuel and marketing businesses; much of its revenue and earnings come from fuel and energy activities. Berkshire Hathaway held a 38.6% interest through January 31, 2023, accounting for it under the equity method and including its share of PTC earnings in equity-method earnings. After acquiring another 41.4% on that date, Berkshire held an 80% controlling interest and consolidated PTC beginning February 1, 2023. The text reports PTC’s eleven-month 2023 results: revenue $51.739 billion, cost of sales $47.505 billion, operating expenses $2.852 billion, interest expense $414 million, pretax earnings $968 million, income taxes and noncontrolling interests $365 million, and net earnings attributable to Berkshire shareholders $603 million. It also compares PTC’s full-year 2023 and 2022 pretax results: revenues of $56.756 billion and $72.739 billion; cost of sales of $52.196 billion and $67.602 billion; operating expenses of $3.067 billion and $2.583 billion; interest expense of $437 million and $224 million; and pretax earnings of $1.056 billion and $2.330 billion, respectively. The corresponding percentage changes are −22.0%, −22.8%, 18.7%, 95.1%, and −54.7%. 2022 and January 2023 results were not included in Berkshire’s consolidated statements, unlike PTC’s final eleven months of 2023.

nodes.title: PTC and Manufacturing, Service, and Retailing Results
nodes.summary: PTC’s 2023 revenue fell 22% to $56.8 billion amid lower fuel prices, fuel volumes, and in-store sales; fuel sales declined to 16.2 billion gallons. Costs reflected lower fuel prices, while depreciation and amortization rose with acquisition accounting and interest expense increased due mainly to higher rates. Manufacturing, service, and retailing results provide 2021–2023 revenue, pre-tax earnings, taxes and noncontrolling interests, net earnings, tax rates, and margins by business. Earnings exclude specified acquisition-accounting expenses, which are disclosed by year and referenced in other tables. The page also introduces manufacturing’s industrial, building, and consumer products businesses and their revenue and pre-tax earnings breakdown.

nodes.title: Pre-tax earnings as a percentage of revenues
Pre-tax earnings as a percentage of revenues (intro)
nodes.summary: The table reports revenues and pre-tax earnings for industrial, building, and consumer products for 2021–2023, along with totals, percentage changes for 2023 versus 2022 and 2022 versus 2021, and pre-tax earnings as a percentage of revenues. It appears in Management’s Discussion and Analysis under Manufacturing, Service and Retailing.

nodes.title: Industrial products
nodes.summary: The industrial products group comprises PCC aerospace, power and industrial metals; Lubrizol specialty chemicals; IMC metalworking tools; Marmon’s diverse manufacturing, services and leasing businesses; CTB agricultural equipment; Scott Fetzer and LiquidPower products; and, from October 2022, W&W|AFCO structural steel and other acquired manufacturers. In 2023, group revenue rose 13.2%, earnings 16.9%, and earnings margin 0.5 points. PCC grew strongly on aerospace demand and improved efficiency, though energy losses and production-capacity needs remain; Lubrizol revenue fell on weaker volumes and currency, while earnings were flat, with insurance recoveries lower than in 2022; Marmon grew through acquisitions and organic gains, despite weakness in several businesses; and IMC revenue and earnings increased, partly offset by costs, regional weakness and geopolitical effects. In 2022, group revenue and earnings rose 9.4% and 8.8%, while margin slipped 0.1 points. PCC revenue grew with aerospace demand but earnings faced cost and supply pressures; Lubrizol revenue and earnings increased, influenced by pricing, insurance recoveries, fire-related losses, operating disruptions and costs; Marmon grew across most businesses, with higher earnings despite rail leasing weakness and Russia-related losses; IMC revenue increased but earnings declined due to margins, costs, currency and geopolitical impacts.

nodes.title: Building products
nodes.summary: The text describes Berkshire Hathaway’s building products and consumer products groups and their 2023 and 2022 performance. Building products includes homebuilding and lending, flooring, insulation, roofing, masonry, paint, and construction systems. In 2023, group revenue and earnings fell amid higher interest rates and weaker demand; Clayton Homes’ home sales declined, partly offset by higher financial-services income, while other businesses faced lower volumes and efficiencies but benefited from lower input and operating costs. In 2022, revenue and earnings rose on strong demand, higher prices, and improved margins, though rising rates slowed homebuilding late in the year. Consumer products includes vehicles, apparel and footwear, batteries, framing, jewelry, and Jazwares. Its 2023 revenue declined as Forest River and apparel sales weakened, partly offset by Jazwares; RV sales were hurt by rates and inflation, while apparel volumes fell and Duracell revenue was stable.

nodes.title: Consumer products
nodes.summary: The discussion reviews building products results for 2022 versus 2021 and consumer products results for both 2023 versus 2022 and 2022 versus 2021. Building products revenue and earnings rose, driven by strong demand, higher prices, volumes, margins and divestiture gains; rising interest rates slowed housing demand, while Clayton Homes’ sales and loan balances grew but fourth-quarter unit sales and order backlog fell and foreclosures rose. Consumer products includes vehicles, apparel and footwear, batteries, framing, jewelry and acquired toy maker Jazwares. In 2023, revenue fell due to weaker Forest River and apparel sales, partly offset by Jazwares; earnings edged up. In 2022, revenue rose modestly, but earnings declined amid apparel and Duracell pressures from lower volumes, inflation, costs, currency and inventories; Forest River benefited early from sales and pricing before weakening later.

nodes.title: Service and retailing
nodes.summary: The table summarizes revenues, pre-tax earnings, and pre-tax earnings as a percentage of revenues for the service, retailing, and McLane businesses in 2021–2023, with percentage changes for 2023 versus 2022 and 2022 versus 2021. It reports combined revenues of $84.3 billion, $91.5 billion, and $92.6 billion, and combined pre-tax earnings of $4.7 billion, $5.0 billion, and $5.2 billion, respectively.

Presents 2021–2023 revenues, pre-tax earnings, year-over-year changes, and earnings margins for manufacturing groups, plus service, retailing, and McLane. Industrial products’ 2023 growth reflected aerospace demand, acquisitions, and gains at several businesses, with varied pressures; 2022 also grew, but margins edged down. Building products declined in 2023 amid higher rates and weaker demand after strong 2022 results. Consumer products revenue fell in 2023, with earnings slightly higher, following modest revenue growth and lower earnings in 2022. Service, retailing, and McLane combined revenue and earnings rose across the period.

nodes.title: Consumer Products Earnings and Service/Retailing
nodes.summary: The page reviews consumer products group results and introduces service and retailing financial summaries. In 2023, pre-tax earnings rose 3.0%, reflecting Jazwares and stronger apparel and footwear results, partly offset by Forest River and Duracell declines; apparel businesses reduced inventories and resized operations. In 2022, revenues rose 3.1%, while pre-tax earnings fell 23.0% and margins declined to 9.5%. Revenue and earnings drivers included Jazwares, RV sales, apparel and footwear volumes and costs, Duracell sales and currency effects, and Forest River’s changing sales and costs. The service and retailing section lists revenues and pre-tax earnings for Service, Retailing, and McLane.

nodes.title: Pre-tax earnings as a percentage of revenues
Pre-tax earnings as a percentage of revenues (intro)
nodes.summary: The text presents service-group financial results and describes its businesses, including NetJets, FlightSafety, TTI, restaurant and equipment services, logistics, media, WPLG and, since October 2022, IPS. In 2023, revenue rose 8.3% to $20.6 billion, driven by IPS and aviation growth, while TTI revenue fell amid slower orders and high inventories. Pre-tax earnings declined 1.7% to $3.0 billion and margin fell to 14.5%, as weaker TTI and other businesses partly offset aviation and IPS gains. In 2022, revenue increased 19.7% and earnings 14.0%, led by TTI, aviation and IPS; margin declined to 16.0%. The text details revenue and earnings drivers, including activity, rates, margins, costs, currency effects, fuel surcharges and smaller-business gains, and notes expectations that TTI market pressures continue in 2024.

nodes.title: Service
nodes.summary: The service group includes aviation services (NetJets and FlightSafety), electronics distributor TTI, and businesses spanning restaurants, equipment leasing, logistics, news distribution, and television; IPS joined in October 2022. In 2023, revenue rose 8.3% to $1.6 billion higher, including IPS revenue, as aviation services grew but TTI declined amid slowing orders, high inventories, and price competition expected to continue in 2024. Pre-tax earnings fell 1.7% to $3.0 billion, with a lower margin, as TTI and other businesses weakened, partly offset by aviation growth and IPS. In 2022, revenue increased 19.7% and earnings 14.0%, driven mainly by TTI and aviation services, plus IPS and smaller businesses; earnings benefited from sales, margins, training, and lower restructuring costs, while the overall margin declined.

nodes.title: Retailing
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s retailing businesses are led by BHA, an 80-plus-dealership auto retailer offering vehicle sales, service, and related contracts and insurance; home furnishings businesses contribute 18% of retailing revenue, alongside jewelry, candy, kitchenware, party supplies, and motorcycle accessories. In 2023, revenue rose 0.6% as BHA growth offset declines elsewhere, especially home furnishings. BHA vehicle and service results reflected stronger new-car sales, weaker used-car sales, rising supply, and margin pressure; its pretax earnings rose 17.7%, while other retailers’ earnings fell 21.8%. Total pretax earnings were unchanged. In 2022, revenue rose 1.8% as BHA growth offset declines at other retailers; higher vehicle prices and service revenue offset lower unit sales. Pretax earnings fell 4.7% and margin declined, as BHA earnings rose on vehicle margins but other retailers’ earnings fell, particularly in home furnishings, See’s Candies, and Pampered Chef.

nodes.title: McLane
nodes.summary: McLane wholesales grocery, non-food, foodservice and alcoholic beverages; grocery and foodservice have high sales but low margins and depend on major customers, whose reduced purchases could hurt results. In 2023, revenue fell 1.1% to $52.6 billion as grocery and foodservice volumes declined, while beverage revenue rose; pretax earnings increased 67.9% due to improved margins, other income and lower fuel costs, partly offset by personnel expenses. In 2022, revenue rose 7.6% to $53.2 billion and pretax earnings rose 17.8%; growth and slightly better margins were partly offset by higher labor, fuel, insurance and supply-chain costs, including labor and driver shortages and high inventory costs.

nodes.title: Non-Controlled Businesses
nodes.summary: The text reports after-tax earnings from non-controlled investments: gains increased in 2023 mainly due to Occidental, while 2022 growth reflected Kraft Heinz, PTC and Occidental. It gives earnings and impairment-charge figures for Kraft Heinz, Occidental and PTC, noting Occidental’s one-quarter reporting lag and PTC’s transition to consolidation after control was acquired in February 2023. It summarizes investment and derivative gains and losses for 2021–2023, explaining that volatile equity-market revaluations drive results, listing unrealized and realized gains, taxable sale gains, and the PTC fair-value remeasurement gain. Management considers investment gains and losses of limited analytical or predictive value; nearly all equity-index put options have expired, leaving insignificant future exposure.

nodes.title: Other
nodes.summary: The text presents after-tax other earnings for 2021–2023, including acquisition accounting expenses, corporate interest expense, foreign-exchange gains on Berkshire and BHFC debt, and other earnings. Acquisition costs mainly reflect amortization of acquired intangible assets. Currency gains arose as the U.S. dollar strengthened, lowering the dollar value of euro-, pound-, and yen-denominated debt; these gains can be volatile and significant. Other earnings mainly comprise parent-company investment and intercompany interest income, corporate expenses, and unallocated taxes. Investment income rose $483 million in 2023 versus 2022, primarily due to higher interest rates.

Reviews service-group results and drivers for aviation, TTI, IPS and smaller businesses; retailing, including BHA and home furnishings; and McLane, covering revenue, pre-tax earnings, margins, operating conditions, costs and 2024 outlook. It also reports after-tax results from non-controlled investments, related impairments and volatile investment and derivative gains or losses, including PTC’s consolidation and management’s view of their limited predictive value. Other earnings include acquisition amortization, corporate interest and expenses, foreign-exchange effects on debt, taxes, and higher investment income.

nodes.title: Management’s Discussion and Analysis Financial Condition
nodes.summary: Berkshire reported strong liquidity and a $561.3 billion equity base at year-end 2023, up $87.8 billion; net earnings were $96.2 billion, including $58.9 billion in after-tax investment gains, which have caused earnings volatility. It repurchased $9.2 billion of shares under a flexible, indefinite program, subject to a $30 billion minimum liquidity threshold. Cash and Treasury bills totaled $163.3 billion; securities holdings, equity transactions, and PTC acquisitions are detailed. The discussion covers $128.3 billion of borrowings, issuance, repayments, debt balances and maturities for Berkshire, BHFC, BNSF, BHE and PTC, including guarantees and foreign-exchange effects. Businesses generated $37–49 billion in annual operating cash flow over three years; 2023 capital spending was $19.4 billion, with $14.3 billion forecast for BNSF and BHE in 2024, and BHE acquired an additional Cove Point interest.

nodes.title: Contractual Obligations and Insurance Loss Estimates
key_items: Management’s Discussion and Analysis Contractual Obligations
Property and casualty insurance unpaid losses
nodes.summary: The page summarizes future debt interest, lease and aircraft repurchase payments, insurance claim obligations, and major purchase and capital commitments, noting payment estimates, uncertainty, and expected funding from operating cash flows. It explains that significant accounting estimates may change as facts emerge, then describes how unpaid property and casualty losses are estimated for reported and IBNR claims, how claim-tail length and litigation vary by claim type, and that $146 billion in liabilities was recorded at year-end 2023, 76% for GEICO and Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group.

Reviews Berkshire’s 2021–2023 insurance results, including GEICO’s premiums, claims, policy trends, catastrophe losses, reserves and expenses; Berkshire Hathaway Primary Group’s businesses, growth, underwriting results and long-tail claim risks; and Reinsurance Group’s property/casualty, life/health, retroactive reinsurance, periodic-payment annuities and run-off variable annuities. It also covers insurance investment income, float and fixed-income holdings; BNSF railroad operations and results; Berkshire Hathaway Energy’s businesses and performance; Pilot Travel Centers’ consolidation and results; manufacturing, service and retailing businesses and earnings drivers; financial condition, liquidity, investments, debt, capital spending and commitments; and insurance loss-estimation methods and liabilities.

nodes.title: GEICO
Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group
nodes.summary: The text explains GEICO’s and Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group’s (BHRG) unpaid-loss reserving methods, uncertainties, and 2023 reserve changes. GEICO estimates claim frequency and severity using actuarial models and case development; reserves fell $1.5 billion in 2023, while a 1% change in bodily-injury severity could change liabilities by $210 million. BHRG’s property and casualty reserves are detailed by category, with discussion of ceding-company data limitations, reporting delays, coverage disputes, case reviews, and IBNR estimation methods. It describes approaches for short- and long-tail claims, 2023 workers’ compensation and other casualty reserve reductions, sensitivity estimates for assumptions, and asbestos/environmental liabilities and uncertainty.

nodes.title: Retroactive reinsurance
nodes.summary: Retroactive reinsurance covers pre-inception losses, mainly long-tail casualty and liability claims. At year-end 2023, gross unpaid losses were $34.6 billion and deferred charges $9.5 billion; maximum remaining gross losses are expected not to exceed $50 billion, with limited potential development absent major legal changes. Loss estimates use contract-level exposure, trends, scenarios, payment activity, and ceding-company information, with reassessment when conditions change. Asbestos and environmental liabilities were about $12.2 billion; incomplete claims data and legal or regulatory changes complicate estimates. Deferred charges are amortized with expected claim payments; 2024 expense is estimated at $900 million. Fourth-quarter estimate increases of $1.1 billion for prior-year contracts resulted in a $650 million net pre-tax underwriting loss.

nodes.title: Other Critical Accounting Estimates
nodes.summary: The company reports $84.6 billion in goodwill and $18.9 billion in indefinite-lived intangible assets at December 31, 2023. It tests them for impairment annually and when circumstances indicate possible impairment, estimating fair value primarily through discounted earnings or cash flows and using forecasts, discount rates, and other assumptions. These estimates require significant judgment and are uncertain; excess carrying values are charged to earnings, subject to goodwill limits. The company concluded goodwill was not impaired, but COVID-19’s long-term effects and economic uncertainty may cause wide variations in fair value estimates.

nodes.title: Other Critical Accounting Estimates
nodes.summary: The 2023 annual goodwill impairment review found nine reporting units whose estimated fair values were less than 20% above carrying values. PCC was valued at $32.6 billion, 10% above its $29.7 billion carrying value, including $7.5 billion of goodwill. PTC, Jazwares, and IPS had combined fair values of $21.5 billion, 1.5% above carrying values, with $8.5 billion of goodwill. The remaining five units had estimated fair values of $4.4 billion, about 10% above carrying values, including $1.3 billion of goodwill.

nodes.title: Market Risk Disclosures
Equity Price Risk
nodes.summary: The document outlines market risks affecting fair values of assets and liabilities, chiefly equity prices, interest rates, foreign exchange, and commodities, noting volatile investment portfolios. Equity risk is emphasized: equity securities are the largest investment category, holdings favor well-managed businesses and are often concentrated in a few issuers; five companies represented about 79% of equity fair value at year-end 2023. Long holding periods, expected short-term volatility, and capital and liquidity buffers are discussed. A table gives equity holdings excluding Kraft Heinz and Occidental, and estimated effects of hypothetical 30% price changes in 2023 and 2022 on fair value and after-tax net earnings; the scenarios are not worst-case outcomes, and declines could be more severe.

nodes.title: Interest Rate and Foreign Currency Risks
nodes.summary: Describes interest-rate-sensitive investments and debt, the company’s approach to credit risk and borrowing costs, and its limited use of derivatives or maturity matching. It explains how market rates and other factors affect fair values and presents hypothetical rate-change sensitivity estimates for assets and liabilities at December 31, 2023 and 2022, noting the assumptions and limitations. It also outlines foreign-currency exposure from international operations, transactions, and multinational-stock investments, with little currency matching or derivative hedging.

nodes.title: Market Risks and Internal Controls
nodes.summary: Describes foreign-currency exposure and 2023/2022 after-tax effects on earnings and other comprehensive income; commodity price risks, customer pricing as mitigation, and limited use of derivatives; directs readers to Item 7 market-risk disclosures. Management reports its evaluation found financial-reporting controls effective at December 31, 2023, using the COSO 2013 framework, and notes Deloitte & Touche audited their effectiveness.

The section covers market risks to asset and liability values from equity prices, interest rates, foreign currencies, and commodities. It describes concentrated equity holdings, investment horizons and liquidity buffers, and hypothetical equity-price and interest-rate sensitivity estimates with assumptions and limitations. It outlines currency exposure from operations and investments, limited hedging and maturity matching, commodity risks and customer pricing mitigation, and related earnings and comprehensive-income effects. It also reports effective financial-reporting controls under the COSO 2013 framework as of year-end 2023, audited by Deloitte & Touche.

nodes.title: Market Risks and Internal Control
key_items: Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
Management’s Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: Describes foreign-currency exposure and reports after-tax exchange-rate effects for 2023 and 2022, including impacts on earnings and other comprehensive income. Explains commodity price exposure, efforts to pass costs to customers, and limited use of derivatives. Directs readers to Item 7 for further market-risk disclosures. Reports management’s assessment that internal control over financial reporting was effective as of December 31, 2023, under the COSO 2013 framework, and notes Deloitte & Touche’s audit.

Covers GEICO and Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group loss-reserving methods, uncertainties, sensitivities, and 2023 reserve changes, including retroactive reinsurance, asbestos and environmental liabilities, and deferred charges. Reviews goodwill and indefinite-lived intangible impairment testing, key reporting-unit valuations, assumptions, and uncertainty. Discusses market risks from equity prices, interest rates, currencies, and commodities, related exposures, mitigations, and sensitivity effects, then reports effective internal controls under the COSO framework and Deloitte’s audit before directing readers to the financial statements.

summary: Explains the risks and non-guaranteed nature of Berkshire’s forward-looking statements, factors that could cause actual results to differ, and its NYSE-listed shares. Covers shareholders, dividends, repurchases, and stock-performance comparisons, then presents 2021–2023 results by business and management’s decentralized structure. Discusses insurance underwriting, investments, reserves, float and GEICO, reinsurance and primary insurance; railroad, energy, Pilot, manufacturing, service and retail operations; financial condition, liquidity, debt, capital spending and commitments; impairment testing, market risks, internal controls and the financial statements. Item 6 is reserved.

title: REPORT OF INDEPENDENT REGISTERED PUBLIC ACCOUNTING FIRM

nodes.title: Independent Auditor’s Report
key_items: Opinions on the Financial Statements and Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: The auditor reports unqualified opinions that Berkshire Hathaway’s 2022–2023 balance sheets and 2021–2023 financial statements fairly present its financial position, results, and cash flows under U.S. GAAP, and that internal financial controls were effective at year-end 2023. The report notes adoption of a long-duration insurance contracts accounting standard in 2023. It outlines management’s and auditor’s responsibilities, auditor independence, PCAOB standards, and procedures to assess misstatement risks, examine evidence, evaluate accounting, estimates and presentation, and test internal controls; the auditor considers the work a reasonable basis for its opinions.

nodes.title: Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: Internal control over financial reporting provides reasonable assurance that financial records accurately reflect company transactions and asset dispositions, transactions and receipts and expenditures are properly authorized and recorded under GAAP, and unauthorized use or disposal of assets with a potentially material financial impact is prevented or detected promptly. Such controls may not prevent or detect all misstatements, and future effectiveness may decline as conditions change or compliance deteriorates.

nodes.title: Critical Audit Matters

title: POLICY RELATING TO RECOVERY OF ERRONEOUSLY AWARDED COMPENSATION
summary: Adopted December 1, 2023, this policy requires executive officers, to the fullest extent permitted by law, to repay or forfeit qualifying performance-based awards received on or after that date when awards tied to financial results are affected by a material securities-law reporting noncompliance restatement involving SEC filings on or after October 2, 2023, and three-year lookback compensation exceeds the restated amount. The Board may also require recovery when it deems it in the Company’s and shareholders’ best interests. Independent directors have final, binding authority over applicability and recovery amounts. Award documents incorporate the policy, and recovery remedies are nonexclusive.
